## ZEPA on the way: the European recognition that consolidates protection

The file that has been sitting in the offices of the Regional Ministry of Sustainability and Environment of the Junta de Andalucía has been accumulating technical reports, updated cartography, and bird censuses for months. La Charca de Suárez aspires to become a Special Protection Area for Birds, a legal designation that emanates directly from the European Union Birds Directive and that, if the planned deadlines are met, will be formalized during 2025. The procedure is not a mere administrative formality: it constitutes the official recognition that this Motril wetland hosts bird populations whose conservation is a priority for the entire continent.

The ZEPA declaration will substantially change the legal status of the site. Until now, la Charca de Suárez appears in the Inventory of Wetlands of Andalusia and holds the category of Special Conservation Area, a designation focused on the protection of habitats and species of flora and fauna. The new classification adds a layer of specifically ornithological protection, which will require any project that could affect the area to undergo more rigorous impact assessments. Public administrations will have to justify with solid data any intervention that alters the balance of the ecosystem.

The practical value of the European designation transcends the regulatory sphere. Inclusion in the ZEPA network opens the door to community funding lines aimed at the management of protected areas, funds that can finance everything from scientific monitoring programs to ecological restoration actions. For a municipality like Motril, which has invested more than 1.5 million euros in the last four years, the possibility of attracting European resources represents considerable budgetary relief and an incentive to maintain the pace of investment without relying exclusively on municipal coffers.

The technicians who have driven the file forward emphasize the ornithological uniqueness of the site. La Charca de Suárez functions as a refuge for dozens of migratory species that find in this corner of the Granada coast a resting point on their routes between Europe and Africa. The ZEPA declaration would consolidate the wetland's role as a node within the European ecological network Natura 2000, a mesh of interconnected spaces that guarantees the survival of birds on a continental scale. Without that network, local conservation efforts would remain isolated and lose effectiveness.

The declaration process requires the preparation of a standardized data form detailing the species present, their populations, and the conservation status of the habitat. That document, which is already being reviewed by the technical services of the Junta, will serve as the basis for the management plan that will accompany the protection designation. The plan will establish the specific conservation measures, permitted uses, and limitations on human activity within the protected perimeter, an instrument that will provide legal certainty to both the managers of the space and neighboring landowners.

The processing includes a period of public information during which any citizen or organization may submit objections. That step, far from being a formality, has demonstrated in other Andalusian files its capacity to enrich the final documents with contributions from conservation groups, neighborhood associations, and affected economic sectors. In the case of la Charca, the expectation is that the process will develop without major controversy, given the broad social consensus that the protection of the wetland has generated in Motril over the last two decades.

The coexistence of protection designations is not an administrative anomaly but a deliberate strategy. The ZEC protects habitats: the tamarisk groves, the reed beds, the freshwater surfaces that sustain unique flora. The ZEPA will protect the birds that depend on those habitats, creating a comprehensive guardianship system that covers both the stage and the main actors of the ecosystem. That double coverage makes la Charca de Suárez one of the most solidly protected natural areas on the Andalusian Mediterranean coast.

The calendar being handled by the regional administration points to the formal declaration taking place before the end of 2025. The approval will correspond to the Governing Council of the Junta de Andalucía, which must ratify the proposal submitted by the competent regional ministry. Once the agreement is published in the Official Bulletin of the Junta de Andalucía, la Charca de Suárez will join the list of Andalusian ZEPAs, a network that already exceeds fifty sites and constitutes one of the most extensive in Europe.

The European recognition arrives at a particularly opportune moment. The recent inauguration of the Interpretation Center, the incorporation of new technicians, and the improvement works on the surrounding area have prepared the ground for la Charca to assume a more ambitious role as a reference environmental facility on the Granada coast. The ZEPA will provide the institutional and financial backing needed to ensure that this qualitative leap does not remain a mere declaration of intent.

The ornithologists who have frequented the wetland for years receive the news with a mixture of satisfaction and prudence. They know that legal protection does not by itself guarantee effective conservation, but they recognize that without it, any progress remains exposed to political fluctuations and urban development pressures that have historically threatened the wetlands of the Andalusian coast. The ZEPA shields the future of la Charca against contingencies that, in other times, would have proved fatal for a site of these characteristics.

The ongoing file also requires updating the inventories of waterbirds that use the wetland as a wintering area or as a migratory stopover. These censuses, carried out by specialized technicians and volunteers from conservation organizations, will provide updated data on species such as the purple heron, the common moorhen, or the little bittern, birds whose presence in la Charca more than justifies the declaration. The information gathered during recent migratory cycles reinforces the scientific argumentation supporting the proposal.

The ZEPA declaration will not imply significant restrictions for the current uses of the surrounding area, given that la Charca de Suárez has already functioned as a de facto protected natural area for years. Environmental education activities, scientific research, and regulated public use will continue to develop normally, now under a more solid legal umbrella. Municipal officials are confident that the new designation will also attract a profile of visitor specifically interested in birdwatching, a growing tourism segment throughout Andalusia.

The road to ZEPA has been long and not without obstacles. La Charca de Suárez survived decades of urban development pressure, agricultural pollution, and institutional neglect before becoming the natural area it is today. The European declaration represents the culmination of a recovery process that began with citizen mobilization and now receives the definitive backing of community institutions. For those who have followed the wetland's evolution since its worst moments, the ZEPA seal has a symbolic value that is difficult to quantify.

The Junta de Andalucía is simultaneously processing the updating of the cartographic boundaries of the protected area, a technical adjustment that will allow the incorporation of small adjoining plots that have gained ecological value in recent years. That perimeter review, although minor in terms of surface area, demonstrates that the regional administration views la Charca de Suárez as a living and expanding space, not as a site frozen in time. The ZEPA will be born with boundaries adjusted to the current ecological reality of the wetland.

The European recognition will definitively consolidate la Charca de Suárez as the natural jewel of the Granada coast, a status already claimed by the Motril City Council but which will now have the endorsement of community legislation. The combination of reinforced legal protection, European funding, and committed local management paints a promising scenario for a wetland that has managed to rise from its ashes. The file continues its course and, barring unforeseen events, 2025 will be the year la Charca de Suárez debuts its status as a Special Protection Area for Birds.
